title: ChIP-Atlas 2025 update: 10-year anniversary of a data-mining platform for exploring epigenomic landscape.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: HEAD: experimentList.tab 359,471,390 bytes and fileList.tab 126,917,161 bytes (both over the 50 MB cap, so only byte-range samples taken); analysisList.tab 210,378 bytes (downloaded, 6,364 rows, TF / cell-type / evidence / genome-build columns). Byte-range samples of experimentList.tab at four offsets: 3 MB from the start gave 6,760 complete rows, all ce10 (worm), 0 malformed processing-log fields; 2 MB samples at 120, 200 and 300 MB offsets gave 4,504 mm9, 2,467 mm10 and 5,512 hg38 rows. Columns seen: SRX/DRX/ERX experiment ID, genome build, curated antigen class, curated antigen, curated cell-type class, curated cell type, cell-type description, a 'reads,%mapped,%duplicates,peak count' field, submission title, then a variable number (13 to 30 total fields) of free-text submitter key=value attributes. 'Unclassified' or 'No description' antigen class: 2,899/6,760 ce10 rows, 742+321/4,504 mm9 rows, 694/5,512 hg38 rows. Downloaded one peak file, hg38 bed05/SRX10829255.05.bed (1,076,386 bytes, 12,629 peaks, MACS2 narrowPeak-style 10 columns). Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.17959610 is a code archive only (11.3 MB, MIT licence). Europe PMC supplementaryFiles timed out once; not retried.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The total of 464,655 experiments (Table 1) and the >460,000 figure; that curation is manual but CNN- (convolutional neural network) and SVM- (support vector machine) assisted since ~2019; the new QC (quality control) panels and bigWig correlation clustering; the FANTOM CAGE enhancer/promoter tracks (447,315 human, 288,877 mouse). I did not count the full experimentList rows, so the file-vs-paper count (rows are repeated per genome build, e.g. hg19 and hg38) is unverified.

a1_downloadable.note: Verified: all metadata and peak files served over plain HTTPS from chip-atlas.dbcls.jp with no login (HTTP 200 on every HEAD).

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Verified in file: curated antigen class, antigen, cell-type class and cell type are explicit columns next to the raw submitter free text. For a sequence-to-binding task the label would instead have to be constructed from peak BEDs; that variant is not proposed.

a3_inputs_present.note: Verified: the input text (submission title plus submitter key=value attributes such as 'cell type=embryonic stem cell') sits in the same row; no lookups needed.

a4_units_stated.note: Classification target, so units are mostly moot. The processing-log field packs reads, % mapped, % duplicates and peak count into one comma string; units are implied, not in the file header (documentation on the GitHub wiki not checked).

a5_enough_rows.note: Full row count not taken (359 MB file over cap). Byte-range samples alone held 19,243 complete rows across 4 genome builds; ~460k experiments claimed in the paper.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Metadata task needs only the 359 MB table. The peak/bigWig side of ChIP-Atlas is terabyte-scale and would fail A6; it is not used.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Not fully verified: rows repeat per genome build, so the file will exceed 464,655 rows; deduplicating on experiment ID should reconcile it. No contradiction observed, but count unconfirmed.

a8_label_provenance.note: Labels are human curation of the same free text the model reads, which is the intended task, not leakage. Caution (paper text): curation has been CNN- and SVM-assisted since ~2019, and there is no flag marking which rows were model-suggested, so recent labels are partly another model's output.

B1.why: One table, one row per experiment per genome build; verified in byte-range samples.

B2.why: Tab-separated but ragged: 13 to 30 fields per row with free-text key=value tails; needs a custom parser. Seen in files.

B3.why: One curation scheme by one team across all builds; class vocabularies consistent across the four samples I read.

B4.why: 'Unclassified'/'No description' common (43% of ce10 sample rows for antigen); easy to drop or use as unlabeled set.

B5.why: Same experiment repeated across genome builds (hg19/hg38, mm9/mm10); dedupe on ID is trivial. Inferred from file structure.

B6.why: Columns readable by inspection; formal column documentation (GitHub wiki) not opened by me.

C1.why: Transfer question (human/mouse curation to worm/fly, old to new submissions) is informative; but 'string match suffices' is a likely dull outcome.

C2.why: ChIP-Atlas's own CNN/SVM curators (code not checked), LLM curation tools (Metappuccino, GPT-4o annotation); EpiClass predicts metadata from signal, not text.

C3.why: Weak 'better' angle: open, honestly split text classifier on 6 organisms of curated labels; none retrieved does exactly this.

C4.why: Manual curation of thousands of new experiments monthly is costly, but already partly automated by the authors.

C5.why: Obvious dummies: majority class and exact string match of submitter 'cell type' attribute to curated label.

D1.why: BiomedBERT/PubMedBERT and small sentence-embedding models are open weights for biomedical text.

D2.why: Short texts; embed unique strings once on CPU, then fit logistic regression head.

D3.why: BiomedBERT MIT-licensed; ChIP-Atlas code MIT (Zenodo record checked); data openly served.

E1.why: Hold out by genome/organism or by submission title (study proxy); columns present in file.

E2.why: Six-plus organisms and thousands of distinct submission titles visible in samples.

E3.why: Majority class and string-match baselines computable directly from the table.

E4.why: No replicate curations or curator-disagreement data; noise floor unknowable from this file alone.

E5.why: Rows whose submitter attribute literally names the curated cell type must be predicted near-perfectly.

E6.why: Label shuffling and dropping the title vs attribute blocks are straightforward.

E7.why: Temporal proxy via accession order and ENA-FIRST-PUBLIC dates seen in some rows; Cistrome DB curations as external labels (not opened).

E8.why: No published accuracy for ChIP-Atlas's CNN/SVM curators was retrieved.

G1.why: SRX/ERX/DRX experiment accessions and genome build present in every row; seen in files.

G2.why: Cistrome DB curated factor/cell annotations are plausible partners; SRX-to-GSM mapping needed, not checked.

G3.why: One experiment maps to one GEO sample usually, but build duplication must be collapsed first.

G4.why: Two independent curations would show where human labels disagree; marginal over either alone.

H1.why: Multiclass: all antigen and cell-type classes present; 'Unclassified' rows record where curators failed.

H2.why: Thousands of submitting labs, six-plus organisms, four assay types in the samples I read.

H4.why: Paper says no quality filtering and ML-assisted curation, but which rows are model-suggested is hidden.

I1.why: ChIP-Atlas team (Oki lab, Kumamoto) and Cistrome DB curators do this job monthly.

I2.why: Could replace or triage their curation step, but they already have CNN/SVM helpers.

I3.why: Their decision is accept/edit a suggestion; top-k accuracy on hard rows matches roughly.

I4.why: Exact string matching may solve most rows; ML only helps on the messy tail. Untested.

J1.why: Text classification with grouped splits; little genomics modelling.

J2.why: Cell-type and antigen names are easy to sanity-check by eye.

J3.why: String-match baseline accuracy is itself a shareable finding about curation difficulty.

J4.why: No budget stated; a week seems enough.

J5.why: Informal kill condition proposed in cheapest_killing_check; not yet written to NOTES.md.

existing_models.name: ChIP-Atlas internal CNN- and SVM-assisted curation (Table 1 of this paper)
existing_models.score_and_split: No accuracy or split reported in this paper.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Paper names variable data quality and missing quality information as the open problem, not curation.

existing_models.name: EpiClass (bioRxiv 2025.09.04.670545), classifiers on epigenomic signal
existing_models.score_and_split: ~98% assay accuracy on 47,065 ChIP-Atlas signal files; sex 82%, cancer status 88%, biomaterial 91% agreement with provided labels (signal input, not text).
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Life-stage classifier poorly calibrated on public data; performance varies by source; best on data like the training distribution.

existing_models.name: Metappuccino (bioRxiv 2025.10.31.685769), LLM reconstruction of SRA metadata
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved; abstract only says it infers 19 metadata classes from free text for cancer studies.

existing_models.name: GPT-4o annotation of cell lines and mouse strains (Database 2026, baag041)
existing_models.score_and_split: 77% of mouse-strain and 59% of cell-line GEO experiments correctly annotated, zero-shot plus retrieval.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not read beyond the abstract snippet.

backbone.name: BiomedBERT (PubMedBERT) or a small sentence-embedding model, frozen, plus logistic-regression head
backbone.licence: MIT (BiomedBERT); ChIP-Atlas code MIT; data openly served (no explicit data licence seen)

integration.join_key: SRX experiment accession mapped to GEO GSM sample
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Where do two independent expert curation teams disagree about the same public experiment, and can a text model flag those rows for re-curation?

controls.positive_control: Rows whose submitter 'cell type=' or 'cell line=' attribute string exactly equals the curated cell type must be predicted near-perfectly; antigen class 'Input control' from titles containing 'input'.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle labels within genome build and confirm collapse to the majority-class baseline; drop the title block and the attribute block in turn.
controls.external_validation: Train on human and mouse, test on worm/fly/yeast/rat rows; or train on older accessions and test on newer ones; optionally Cistrome DB labels for overlapping experiments.

honest_claim_h3: Predicts the cell-type and antigen class that the ChIP-Atlas curators (partly assisted by their own CNN/SVM tools) would assign from the free text submitters wrote to SRA, for experiments curators could classify at all.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use the free-text descriptions scientists submit with public epigenomics experiments to predict the standardized cell type and target protein that expert curators assigned.
plain_idea.train_on: Per experiment: the submission title and submitter key=value notes (e.g. 'tissue=whole', 'genotype=...'). Roughly 460,000 experiments per the paper; I counted 19,243 rows in partial samples only.
plain_idea.predict: The curated cell-type class and antigen (protein or histone mark) class, which ChIP-Atlas curators assigned by reading the same text, partly with machine help.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Curation teams like ChIP-Atlas and Cistrome process thousands of new experiments a month; knowing how much a simple string match already solves tells them where human effort is still needed.

pitch.headline: Hundreds of thousands of public epigenomics experiments with curated cell-type and target labels sitting next to the raw submitter text, in one 359 MB table.
pitch.what_makes_the_data_unusual: Same curation scheme across at least 4 genome builds (ce10, mm9, mm10, hg38 seen) from one team; raw text and label in the same row; 'Unclassified' rows (2,899 of 6,760 in the worm sample) mark hard cases.
pitch.the_win: A frozen text-embedding classifier that clearly beats exact string matching on held-out organisms, for example on worm and fly rows when trained on human and mouse. No published baseline accuracy exists to cite.
pitch.even_if_it_fails: We learn what fraction of curation is solved by string matching alone, which is a useful one-page note for the curators.
pitch.who_wants_it: The ChIP-Atlas team (Oki lab, Kumamoto University) and Cistrome DB curators, deciding whether to automate or triage monthly metadata curation.

ml_idea: Parse experimentList.tab, deduplicate experiment IDs across genome builds, embed title plus submitter attributes once with a frozen biomedical text model, and fit a logistic-regression head for curated cell-type class and antigen class; evaluate with organism-held-out and accession-order (temporal) splits against majority-class and exact-string-match baselines.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed: about 460k experiments, far fewer unique text strings, embedded at roughly 50 to 100 short texts per second on CPU; linear head CV in minutes.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Download experimentList.tab (359 MB), deduplicate on experiment ID, and score an exact-string-match baseline (submitter cell-type attribute vs curated cell type) on held-out submissions; if it exceeds ~90% accuracy on classifiable rows, there is no ML project.

verdict_reason: The data is open and the label column is real, but the only laptop-sized task (text to curated metadata) is low-impact. String matching may solve it, LLM curation tools already exist, and the labels are partly CNN/SVM-assisted. The genomic side (peaks, signal) is terabyte-scale and its sequence-to-binding task is crowded.
